title: Finite-temperature Lanczos for anisotropic spin systems using triple-hybrid high-performance computing
abstract: Lanczos concepts are often realized on supercomputers. In view of modern architectures of high-performance computing triple-hybrid schemes employing MPI, CPU-openMP as well as GPU-openMP should be utilized. The present article sketches how such a scheme could be utilized in order to meet the demands of the finite-temperature Lanczos method for anisotropic spin systems.
summary: This paper details a computational methodology to simulate anisotropic spin systems at finite temperatures by employing the Finite-Temperature Lanczos Method (FTLM). It overcomes severe scaling limitations by designing and implementing a highly parallelized, triple-hybrid high-performance computing scheme utilizing MPI, OpenMP, and GPUs. The work demonstrates its feasibility on complex molecular magnets like $	ext{Mn}_9$, providing insights into their magnetic properties.
main_problem: To apply the finite-temperature Lanczos method (FTLM) to study anisotropic spin systems whose Hilbert spaces are too large for exact diagonalization.
main_result: The authors successfully sketched a framework utilizing a triple-hybrid HPC scheme (MPI/CPU/GPU) to tackle the computational demands of FTLM for these complex magnetic models, demonstrating feasibility on systems like Mn9.
method: The core method is the Finite-Temperature Lanczos Method (FTLM), which approximates thermodynamic expectation values using trace estimators. The implementation heavily relies on parallelizing sparse matrix-vector multiplications across MPI ranks, CPU threads, and GPU engines.
model_or_system: The study focuses on anisotropic spin systems governed by a Hamiltonian including Heisenberg exchange, single-ion anisotropies, Zeeman terms, and dipolar interactions. Examples include fictitious ring molecules and $	ext{Mn}_9$ clusters.
key_observables: Heat capacity ($C$), Magnetic Susceptibility ($\chi_M T / B$), and low-energy density of states.
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta = 1/k_B T$) and applied magnetic field strength ($B$).
main_assumptions: The primary approximation is the use of FTLM itself. The authors also discuss using an improved, symmetric form ($s$FTLM) despite its increased computational cost.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the parallel steps (MPI-step 1 and 2) of matrix-vector multiplication on a distributed memory architecture. Other figures show calculated heat capacity and susceptibility for model systems like the ring molecule and $	ext{Mn}_9$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem, details the mathematical framework (FTLM approximations), outlines the necessary computational infrastructure (triple-hybrid HPC scheme), and then presents results on specific spin models ($	ext{Mn}_9$, ring system) to validate the approach.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses simulating quantum magnetism in large molecular clusters using state-of-the-art high-performance computing techniques, which is crucial for understanding magnetic materials beyond simple lattice models.

Heat capacity of a fictitious spin ring of N = 6 spins with s = 5/2 with nearest-neighbor Heisenberg exchange, strong single-ion easy-axis anisotropy as well as all-to-all dipo- lar interaction for B = 0.1 T (top) and B = 1 T (bottom). τ = 1 or 0 denotes the use or not-use of time reversed random vectors; NL provides the number of Lanczos steps for a single random vector, and R gives the number of employed random vectors according to (8) and (9).

Figure 3 shows as a first result the heat capacity for two values of the magnetic field applied along the z-axis which is the symmetry axis of the ring. The various curves ori- gin from using time reversed random vectors (τ = 1) or not (τ = 0) together with NL Lanczos steps for each ran- dom vector and averages of the partition function over R random vectors according to (8) and (9). One notices that the heat capacity is astonishingly robust and well approximated by already rather small numbers of ran- dom vectors and Lanczos steps of the order of 100.
